title: NASA Tests Mars Helicopter Blades Faster Than Sound
summary:
Flying a helicopter on Mars is very hard, because the air there is only about 1% as thick as Earth's air. The blades have almost nothing to push against, so they must spin very fast — so fast their tips can go faster than sound.

In March, NASA engineers tested new blades at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, spinning them in a big chamber filled with carbon dioxide to copy the thin Martian air. In 137 test runs, the blades held together even as their tips raced past the speed of sound.

One three-blade rotor reached 3,750 spins per minute, and a second two-blade rotor from NASA's SkyFall project reached 3,570. A fan blowing headwinds pushed the tips to Mach 1.08 on the final runs — faster than sound.

NASA aerodynamicist Shannah Withrow-Maser said the team had only hoped for Mach 1.05.

NASA's first Mars helicopter, Ingenuity, flew on April 19, 2021, as the first aircraft on another world, but its blades were limited to 2,700 spins per minute. Future helicopters could carry heavier science gear and scout for future missions.
why_it_matters: Learning how to fly on Mars helps scientists explore a faraway world, just like learning how things fly helps you understand the world around you.

background_read: A helicopter flies because its spinning blades push against the air, and that push lifts it up.
The air on Mars is very thin, so a helicopter there must spin its blades much faster than one on Earth to get enough lift.
NASA's Ingenuity was the first helicopter to fly on another world, and engineers are now testing stronger blades for bigger helicopters that could carry more science gear.
